quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Bilingualism and Attention: What the Evidence Shows] For two decades, a popular claim has held that growing up with two languages strengthens children's "executive function", the set of mental skills used to focus attention, switch between tasks, and ignore distractions. The idea is plausible: a bilingual child must constantly select one language and suppress the other. Early studies seemed to confirm it. In a widely cited experiment, bilingual children outperformed monolingual peers on a task requiring them to sort cards by color and then, abruptly, by shape. Later work complicated the picture. A large analysis combining results from many studies found that the average advantage was small, and that it shrank further in the better-designed studies, which controlled for differences in family income and parents' education. Researchers also noted a pattern known as publication bias: studies finding an advantage were more likely to be published than studies finding none. Defenders of the original claim respond that bilingual experience varies enormously, from children who switch languages constantly at home to those who use a second language only at school, and that averaging them together may hide real effects in particular groups. Critics reply that this argument makes the claim difficult to test, since any disappointing result can be explained away. The fair summary is not that bilingualism has no cognitive effects, but that the evidence for a general attention advantage is weaker than was once believed, and that its benefits to communication and cultural understanding do not depend on the outcome of this debate.
quests.question: Why did later analyses cast doubt on the original claim?
options: Bilingual children performed worse than others in every study.
The original card-sorting experiment could not be repeated at all.
The average advantage was small and shrank in better-controlled studies.
Researchers lost interest and stopped studying bilingual children.
quests.correctAnswer: The average advantage was small and shrank in better-controlled studies.
quests.hint: Look at what the large analysis found, and at what happened in the better-designed studies.
quests.explanation: The combined analysis found a small average advantage that shrank further when studies controlled for family background.
quests.evidenceLine: it shrank further in the better-designed studies

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Memo: Choosing a Venue for the Annual Conference] To: Events Committee. From: Priya Nandakumar. We have narrowed the choice to three venues. The Harbour Hotel has capacity for 320, costs $48,000, and is a ten-minute walk from the main station, but it offers no breakout rooms for parallel sessions. The Lakeside Centre holds 260 and costs $41,000; it has six breakout rooms and free parking, but it is 18 kilometers from the nearest station, and our survey suggests that 40 percent of attendees travel by train. The Old Mill, which costs $39,000 and holds 300, has four breakout rooms and is eight minutes from the station, but its main hall has a pillar that blocks sightlines, and it can offer our preferred dates only if we accept a Sunday finish. Last year's attendance was 285, and registration for this year is running about 5 percent ahead. The program committee has said that at least four parallel sessions are essential. Taking these constraints into account, I recommend the Old Mill. The Harbour Hotel's lack of breakout rooms would force us to cut the parallel sessions, and the Lakeside Centre's capacity leaves too little margin if registrations continue to rise. The Sunday finish and the pillar are real disadvantages, but we can mitigate the first by shortening the closing session and the second by placing the main stage so that the pillar does not block it. I would welcome the committee's views before we sign on Friday.
quests.question: Why is the Harbour Hotel rejected?
options: It is too far from the station.
It cannot host the required parallel sessions.
It is too small for the expected attendance.
It cannot offer the preferred dates.
quests.correctAnswer: It cannot host the required parallel sessions.
quests.hint: Link the program committee's requirement to a feature the hotel lacks.
quests.explanation: The committee says at least four parallel sessions are essential, and the Harbour Hotel has no breakout rooms.
quests.evidenceLine: The Harbour Hotel's lack of breakout rooms would force us to cut the parallel sessions

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Appraiser] Mrs. Teague had brought the vase in a supermarket bag, wrapped in a tea towel, with the care of someone carrying a sleeping child. "It was my mother's," she said. "She always said it was worth a great deal." Gerald turned it over once, then again, and read the mark on the base, which he had read on a hundred identical vases in a hundred identical living rooms. It was a good vase: pleasant, well made, and worth, at auction, perhaps forty dollars. He had been an appraiser for thirty years, and he had learned that the number was only part of the job. "Well," he said slowly, "it's a very fine example of its kind. The glaze on these is rarely so even. Do you know whether your mother ever had it insured?" Mrs. Teague shook her head. "Then I would insure it now," he said, "for a hundred and fifty. Not because anyone's likely to steal it, but because it ought to be treated as something that matters." She thanked him three times and wrapped the vase again in its towel. When she had gone, his assistant looked up from the desk. "A hundred and fifty?" she said. "We both know it's forty." Gerald watched the door close. "Insurance value," he said, "is not auction value. It's what it would cost to replace something that can't be replaced. I wasn't lying. I was estimating the wrong thing, on purpose."
quests.question: What does the phrase "the number was only part of the job" suggest?
options: He does not care about money and works only to please owners.
He is dishonest about prices and tells owners what they want.
He values only expensive objects and ignores the cheap ones.
Part of his job is understanding what an object means to its owner.
quests.correctAnswer: Part of his job is understanding what an object means to its owner.
quests.hint: Think about why an appraiser would care about more than a price.
quests.explanation: The phrase hints that Gerald considers an object's meaning to its owner as well as its market value, as he shows with the vase.
quests.evidenceLine: the number was only part of the job

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Myth of the Self-Made Person] The self-made person is one of the most admired figures in public life: someone who started with nothing and, through effort and talent alone, built a fortune or a career. Such stories are often true as far as they go. People do work hard, and some do overcome daunting disadvantages. The trouble lies in the word 'alone'. Every self-made success relies on things the person did not make: a public school or a library, roads and courts that made commerce possible, customers with money to spend, and often a piece of luck, such as being in the right town when a market opened. None of this diminishes the person's effort. It merely locates it within a larger structure. The distinction matters because the story we tell about success shapes what we think we owe each other. If success is wholly individual, then taxes and public services look like penalties on achievement, and failure looks like a personal defect. If success depends in part on shared institutions, then supporting those institutions looks less like charity and more like maintenance of the conditions that made success possible. One need not reject the value of individual effort to see this. A farmer who works hard still depends on rain. Admiring the farmer's work does not require pretending the rain was her own doing.
quests.question: What is the writer's main point about the phrase "self-made"?
options: It overlooks the shared conditions that success depends on.
It exaggerates how hard successful people really work.
It proves that success is mostly a matter of luck.
It describes people who inherit money and property.
quests.correctAnswer: It overlooks the shared conditions that success depends on.
quests.hint: Focus on the word the writer says is the trouble.
quests.explanation: The writer accepts the effort but says no success is achieved "alone", since schools, roads, courts and customers all contribute.
quests.evidenceLine: The trouble lies in the word 'alone'

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Residents' Association: Proposed Amendments to the Bylaws] The committee proposes three amendments, to be voted on at the annual general meeting on 18 June. The meeting will begin at 7 p.m. in the community hall. Under the current bylaws, any amendment requires approval by two-thirds of members present and voting, provided that at least 40 members are present. Amendment 1 would allow members to vote by proxy, by appointing another member in writing at least 48 hours in advance; no member could hold more than three proxies. Amendment 2 would raise the annual membership fee from $20 to $28, with a reduced fee of $14 for residents over 65. The committee estimates that this would raise about $1,900 a year, which would cover the cost of repairs to the shared courtyard, which have been deferred twice. Amendment 3 would extend the committee's term of office from one year to two, on the grounds that the first year is largely spent learning the role. Critics argue that this would reduce accountability. The committee has responded by proposing that members could call a special meeting to remove any officer if 25 members sign a petition. Members who cannot attend should note that, if Amendment 1 passes, it will apply immediately, but the proxies will not count at the same meeting. Questions may be sent to the secretary by 11 June.
quests.question: At the meeting, 60 members are present and voting. How many must vote in favor for an amendment to pass?
quests.hint: Find two-thirds of the number present and voting.
quests.explanation: Two-thirds of 60 is 40, and the quorum of 40 members present is also met.
quests.evidenceLine: two-thirds of members present and voting

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [A New Battery: Claims and Caveats] A university spin-off has announced a lithium battery that, it says, charges to 80 percent in five minutes and retains 90 percent of its capacity after 2,000 charge cycles. The company's press release describes the technology as "transformative for electric vehicles". The company, founded four years ago by two researchers from the university's materials department, has raised $12 million from investors and says it expects to begin producing cells for carmakers within three years. An independent engineer who reviewed the published data was more measured. First, she noted, the figures came from small laboratory cells, roughly the size of a coin, not from full-size automotive batteries; heat builds up differently in larger packs, and fast charging generates heat. Second, the 2,000-cycle result was achieved at a moderate temperature; batteries in cars operate in conditions ranging from freezing to desert heat. Third, the company reported no data on cost, and the new material includes an expensive metal. None of this suggests the claims are false, she said. The experiments appear to have been carried out carefully. But the distance between a promising laboratory result and a battery that can be manufactured at scale, at a competitive price, is where many such announcements have stalled. "Five minutes is a remarkable number," she said. "I would like to see it again in a car park in July."
quests.question: Which statement best reflects the engineer's attitude toward the announcement?
options: The data have been fabricated.
The battery will certainly transform electric vehicles.
The results are promising but unproven for real-world use.
She has no opinion about the data.
quests.correctAnswer: The results are promising but unproven for real-world use.
quests.hint: Notice what she says about the claims and what she says about the gap that follows.
quests.explanation: She says the claims are not false and the experiments seem careful, but she lists reasons why real-world success is uncertain.
quests.evidenceLine: None of this suggests the claims are false

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [A Treaty in Two Languages] In 1840, a treaty was signed between a colonial government and the chiefs of New Zealand's Maori people, in English and in Maori. The two texts were not identical. The English version stated that the chiefs ceded "sovereignty" to the Crown. The Maori version used a different word, 'kawanatanga', which is closer to 'governorship' and had been used in missionary translations of the Bible to describe the authority of a governor, such as Pontius Pilate. The same Maori text guaranteed the chiefs 'tino rangatiratanga', 'unqualified chieftainship', over their lands and treasures, a phrase stronger than the English guarantee of 'possession'. Historians have argued for generations about what the chiefs understood. Some maintain that they believed they were granting the Crown a limited authority to govern settlers while keeping their own authority. Others point out that the English text was seen by the colonial officials as the legal document and that the discrepancies were not accidental. The disagreement matters because it underlies modern claims about land and self-government. The treaty is now regarded as a founding document, though disagreement over its meaning has never fully disappeared. A tribunal established in 1975 to investigate breaches of the treaty has generally treated both versions as authoritative, and its reports have emphasized the principles of the treaty, such as partnership and protection, rather than the literal words of either text.
quests.question: What is the key difference between the two versions of the treaty?
options: They were signed in different years by different officials and chiefs.
They use different terms for the authority transferred and the authority kept.
They name different groups of chiefs as the signatories of the treaty.
Only the English version mentions the chiefs' lands and treasures at all.
quests.correctAnswer: They use different terms for the authority transferred and the authority kept.
quests.hint: Compare the English word "sovereignty" with the Maori words the passage explains.
quests.explanation: The English text speaks of ceding sovereignty and guaranteeing possession, while the Maori text uses words closer to governorship and unqualified chieftainship.
quests.evidenceLine: closer to 'governorship'

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Email: Re: Marcus's Grade in Physics] Dear Mr. and Mrs. Abdi, Thank you for your message and for the care with which you set out your concerns. I understand that a B-minus is disappointing for a student who has earned an A in every previous science course, and I want to explain both how the grade was reached and what I think would help. Marcus's test scores are strong; his average is 91 percent. The difference lies in the coursework, which counts for 40 percent of the grade. He submitted four of the seven laboratory reports, and the three missing reports were each scored as zero under the department's policy. I recognize that he has had a demanding term, with the debate team and his part-time job, and I did offer him an extension in October and again in December. He did not take either. I am not suggesting that he lacks ability: the reports he did submit were among the best in the class. I am suggesting that the grade reflects the work submitted, and that the pattern is a habit he can change. If he completes the missing reports by 15 January, I am willing to mark them at 70 percent of their value, which would raise his grade to a B-plus. I would also be glad to meet with Marcus and with you.
quests.question: What does the teacher identify as the main reason for the grade?
options: Weak test scores
Strict marking of the tests
Three missing laboratory reports scored as zero
Marcus's participation in the debate team
quests.correctAnswer: Three missing laboratory reports scored as zero
quests.hint: The test average is strong, so look elsewhere in the grade.
quests.explanation: Marcus's tests average 91 percent, but three of the seven reports were not submitted and each counted as zero.
quests.evidenceLine: three missing reports were each scored as zero

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Three Cities, Three Approaches to Household Waste] Hartmoor charges households by the bag: residents buy official bags for general waste, at $2.50 each, while recycling is collected free. In the five years after the system began, the amount of general waste per household fell by 38 percent and recycling rose by 52 percent. However, illegal dumping increased in the first two years, and the council now employs inspectors to check unmarked bags. Valdane collects waste weekly but offers three separate bins, with recycling and food waste collected every week and general waste only every fortnight. Its recycling rate is 61 percent, the highest of the three, but the cost per household is also the highest, $212 a year, because of the additional collection routes. Orsby has the simplest system: one bin for general waste and one for mixed recycling, both collected fortnightly. Its recycling rate is the lowest at 34 percent, though the cost per household is just $98. A study of the three cities found that residents of Orsby were the most likely to say they 'did not know' what could be recycled, and that contamination of recycling with food and non-recyclable items was twice as high there as in Valdane. The study's authors caution against assuming that the best system in one city can be transplanted unchanged to another, since results depend on housing, culture and the cost of enforcement.
quests.question: Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: Hartmoor has the highest recycling rate of the three cities.
Orsby has the highest cost per household of the three cities.
Valdane has the lowest cost per household of the three cities.
Valdane has the highest recycling rate but also the highest cost.
quests.correctAnswer: Valdane has the highest recycling rate but also the highest cost.
quests.hint: Compare the recycling rates and the costs given for each city.
quests.explanation: Valdane's rate is 61 percent, the highest of the three, and its cost of $212 a year is the highest as well.
quests.evidenceLine: Its recycling rate is 61 percent, the highest of the three

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [What a Good Question Does] A bad question seeks an answer; a good question changes what the asker sees. Consider a teacher who asks a class, "What is the capital of France?" The question has a right answer, and once it is given, the matter is closed. Now suppose she asks, "Why do you think capitals are often built beside rivers?" There is no single answer. Some students will talk about trade, others about defense, and a few will notice that the question assumes something that may not be true. The question has not ended a conversation; it has started one. This is why good teachers, interviewers and friends are often distinguished less by what they know than by what they ask. Their questions have a particular quality: they make the other person aware of something they had not thought to examine. They also carry a kind of respect. To ask a genuine question is to admit that you do not already hold the answer, and that the other person might. The risk, of course, is that a question can also be a disguised assertion. "Don't you think it's time we all grew up?" appears to ask something but expects only agreement. The test of a genuine question is whether the asker is prepared to be surprised by the reply. Where that readiness is missing, the question is only a statement wearing a costume, and most people, sooner or later, notice.
quests.question: According to the writer, what distinguishes a good question from a bad one?
options: A good question always has a single, checkable right answer.
A good question changes what the asker sees and opens inquiry.
A good question is difficult for most people to understand.
A good question is always as short and simple as possible.
quests.correctAnswer: A good question changes what the asker sees and opens inquiry.
quests.hint: Look at the sentence that contrasts what each kind of question seeks.
quests.explanation: A bad question seeks an answer and closes the matter, while a good question changes the asker's view and starts a conversation.
quests.evidenceLine: a good question changes what the asker sees
